The People’s Palace: Now With Your Money

Trump promised a “taxpayer‑free” palace. The paperwork says otherwise.

Five months after he knocked down the East Wing to build a ballroom‑plus‑bunker complex, Trump was still telling cameras it would cost “up to $400 million” and that “not 10 cents” would come from taxpayers, all covered by himself and “patriot donors.” 

In reality, his own contractor had already handed the White House a March 5 estimate putting the bill at $600 million — and showing that more than half of it would be paid out of public funds.

Internal summaries obtained by reporters map out the creep in real time. A preliminary estimate in July 2025 put the total at about $270 million, with over $100 million slated to come from the Secret Service and the White House Military Office. As designs expanded, so did the tab: by October, as demolition began, Clark Construction was projecting roughly $478 million, with taxpayers covering nearly half. 

By March this year, the number hit $600 million, with only about $293 million expected from private sources and roughly $307 million from agencies funded by Congress.

To make that math possible, the administration leaned hard on “security.” Emails show White House lawyers tweaking contract language to tie the entire project more closely to protective needs because the Secret Service was being used as a funding vehicle. Secret Service money was budgeted not just for reinforced structures and secure facilities, but for early site prep and even part of the demolition itself. 

Contracting experts who reviewed the documents called that a stretch bordering on abuse of mandate: tearing down the East Wing to pour concrete for a ballroom is a long way from protecting officials from assassination plots.

Public rhetoric never caught up with the internal spreadsheets. Even as invoice logs show tens of millions in federal payments flowing to Clark, Trump kept repeating that the building was a $300–$400 million “donation” from him and unnamed friends, and that the military’s role was limited to unspecified “security enhancements.” The latest White House line is that “President Trump and generous American patriots are funding the ballroom” for around $400 million, while the documents sit there with a $600 million bottom line and government accounts underwriting roughly half of it.

Politically, the project is toxic: polls show most Americans dislike it, and even some Republicans have balked at the idea of quietly routing hundreds of millions through security budgets to finance what critics see as a vanity hall. But institutionally, that is precisely the point. 

By burying the true cost inside agencies whose missions are hard to question — the Secret Service, the Military Office, the Executive Residence — the administration tried to turn a personal monument into a “national security” expense.

On paper, the future presidents’ ballroom is being sold as a privately funded gift to the nation. In the ledgers, it already looks like something much more familiar: a luxury Trump development with the public as involuntary silent partner.

President Donald Trump's White House ballroom project could slap taxpayers with an eye-popping bill.

Instead of the publicly announced $400 million budget, the East Wing renovations will cost $600 million, and taxpayers will pay for part of the project, according to the Washington Post. 

In a statement last July announcing the construction project, the White House said that 
'President Trump and other patriot donors have generously committed to donating the funds necessary to build this approximately $200 million dollar structure.'

Since then, public cost estimates rose to $400 million. 

Trump defended the cost increase in early May, writing on Truth Social, 
'The only reason the cost has changed is because, after deep rooted studies, it is approximately twice the size, and a far higher quality, than the original proposal.'

But a cost summary prepared for the White House in March by Clark Construction, the contractor overseeing the project, estimated the total cost at $600 million, according to the Post.
When asked about the reported disparity in cost projections and the possibility of taxpayer funding, a White House spokesperson said in a statement:
'President Trump and generous American patriots are funding the ballroom to the tune of approximately $400 million.'

The war didn’t just hit oil; it rewired how the global economy thinks about risk, energy and American power.

The first shock is structural. A near‑shutdown of oil and gas flows from the Gulf and a price spike on top of the 2022 shock forced importers in Europe and Asia to confront how exposed they are to a few chokepoints and a handful of producers. 

Some, like Japan and South Korea, slid back into dirtier fuels such as coal to keep the lights on, but the deeper response is acceleration: more renewables, more nuclear, more diversification of suppliers. 

Wind and solar have already reached the point where they can outcompete gas on cost in many markets, and investors now see renewables as projects with payback periods measured in a couple of years instead of decades.

The second shift is geopolitical. The war strained relations inside the oil club, with the U.A.E. walking out of OPEC+ and Saudi Arabia edging closer to Russia, just as sanctions on Moscow were loosened enough to let it cash in on higher prices. 

At the same time, Latin American producers from Brazil to Guyana are racing to expand capacity to capture demand from buyers trying to insure against Middle East instability. 

Overlaying all of this is China, which already dominates manufacturing of solar panels, turbines, grids and batteries; every crisis‑driven renewable build‑out outside the Middle East quietly increases Beijing’s leverage over other countries’ energy security.

Trust is the other casualty. Iran has shown that it can close or tax Hormuz at will, turning a theoretical risk into a practical tool that permanently raises insurance premiums and freight costs. 

Gulf financial and tourist hubs that sold themselves as safe, frictionless platforms now carry the memory of missile strikes on LNG plants, petrochemical complexes, hotels and data centers. 

And the United States, which spent decades presenting its Navy as guarantor of free navigation, has just demonstrated that even its presence cannot ensure uninterrupted passage in a contested strait. 

For investors and policymakers, that translates into a lasting “risk surcharge” on anything tied to the region.

Macro‑economically, the war hit just as the world was beginning to exhale. 

Before the first strikes, global forecasters were preparing to upgrade growth and celebrate fading inflation. Instead, they are now cutting growth projections, watching inflation re‑accelerate and assuming higher interest rates for longer. 

Governments already burdened with large debts are spending more on interest, energy subsidies and defense, leaving less room for long‑term investment. 

Asian economies, hit hardest by supply shocks, are back at development banks’ doors for emergency support.

The war may formally end when a framework is signed, but the economic damage is path‑dependent: more jittery markets, slower growth, higher baseline prices and a world that trusts oil routes, U.S. guarantees and “cheap energy forever” less than it did on February 27.

Others, like Josh Hawley, downplay the need for a vote, focusing instead on the economic relief of reopening the Strait of Hormuz.

For all the talk of peace, the emerging picture is one of a fragile bridge built on promises yet to be detailed. Trump has secured a ceasefire and a pledge to reopen vital shipping lanes, but the core question — whether Iran has truly abandoned its nuclear ambitions — remains unanswered and deferred to a summer of negotiations.
